events.title: Portuguese brazilwood trade
hints: The coast was claimed in 1500 by a fleet bound for India.
Indigenous people cut and carried a dye-yielding tree to European ships in return for trinkets.
The red timber eventually gave the land its name.
events.summary: After Pedro Álvares Cabral's 1500 landfall, Portuguese and French traders obtained brazilwood, used for red dye, by bartering with Indigenous Tupi groups who did the cutting and carrying. The tree's name became the name of the colony.

events.title: Portuguese sugar colony and the slave trade
hints: Hereditary captaincies were granted from 1534, and sugar estates spread along the north-east coast.
About five million Africans were landed here, far more than in any other American colony.
The Portuguese court itself moved here in 1808 before independence in 1822.
events.summary: Portugal began colonising from 1530, and sugar plantations in the north-east used first Indigenous and then mainly enslaved African labour. An estimated five million Africans were forcibly landed during the colonial and imperial periods. Independence from Portugal came in 1822, and slavery was not abolished until 1888.

events.title: Minas Gerais gold and diamond rush
hints: A gold rush in the interior in the 1690s was the first of its scale in the Americas.
Enslaved Africans did most of the mining, and a fifth of the output went to the Crown.
Diamonds found in the 1720s were placed under a royal monopoly.
events.summary: Gold was found in the mountains of Minas Gerais in the 1690s, and the rush brought hundreds of thousands of settlers and enslaved Africans. The Crown took a fifth of the gold and later placed the diamond fields under a tight monopoly. Production declined after the 1760s.

events.title: Dutch Brazil
hints: A trading company seized the richest sugar region of the north-east in 1630.
Under Johan Maurits, a planned city rose at Recife with a stock exchange and an observatory.
Local insurgents, backed by Portugal, expelled the Dutch in 1654.
events.summary: The Dutch West India Company captured Pernambuco in 1630 and governed a large part of the north-east until 1654. It took over sugar mills, expanded the slave trade and built the city of Mauritsstad. Luso-Brazilian revolts drove it out.

events.title: US contingency plan for the 1964 coup
hints: A military takeover in March 1964 ended a left-leaning elected government.
Washington readied a carrier group and fuel supplies, called Operation Brother Sam, in case the coup met resistance.
events.summary: In 1964 the US government prepared Operation Brother Sam, sending naval forces towards the coast to back the generals who overthrew President João Goulart if they met resistance. It proved unnecessary, and US officials welcomed the military regime.
events.quip: The US sent an aircraft carrier to back a coup that did not need one.

events.title: CIA funding of Goulart's opponents
hints: A left-leaning president faced a hostile US administration from the early 1960s.
Covert money flowed to opposition candidates and anti-government groups before the 1962 elections, and the agency also worked in the labour movement.
The covert funding of the 1962 elections in South America's largest country came two years before a 1964 military coup.
events.summary: From 1962 the CIA covertly funded candidates and groups opposed to President João Goulart, spending an estimated several million dollars in the 1962 congressional and state elections, according to declassified records and later testimony. In 1963 the CIA's Richard Helms told a presidential advisory board that the agency was also running covert action in the labour movement. Goulart was overthrown in 1964.
events.quip: Millions went into the 1962 elections, and Goulart still won his 1963 plebiscite in a landslide.
